name: RU-59063
lead: RU-59063 is an experimental nonsteroidal androgen, sometimes classed as a SARM, first described in 1994. It was never marketed and has no clinical use.[1][2]

It was derived from the antiandrogen nilutamide and bound the rat androgen receptor with very high affinity, reported as up to about three times that of testosterone, with little binding to other steroid receptors.[3] Later work showed dose-dependent androgenic activity. It served mainly as a starting point for later antiandrogens such as enzalutamide and apalutamide, and for radioligand research.[1][4]

paras: Wikipedia reports an androgen receptor Ki of about 2.2 nM, with roughly 1,000-fold selectivity over other steroid receptors, and activity initially assumed to be purely antagonistic but later found to include partial androgenic effects.[1] The 1994 study described the arylthiohydantoin series as having exceptionally high receptor affinity and no binding to other steroid receptors, and the lead compound was tritiated for use as a research marker.[3]

Chemists later made iodinated analogues of RU-59063 to develop radioiodinated androgen receptor ligands for imaging.[4][5] Basic-science studies also used it to examine how androgen receptors interact with DNA response elements.[2]
No studies found. All published work is laboratory or animal research on receptor binding and chemistry.

timeline.event: Iodinated analogue developed as an androgen receptor radioligand.[4]

quick.overview:
RU-59063 is an early nonsteroidal compound that binds the androgen receptor very tightly. It was studied in laboratories and never marketed.

Its main significance is as a chemical template for later prostate cancer drugs and imaging agents. No studies of muscle or appearance effects in people exist.
quick.mechanism: It occupies the androgen receptor with higher affinity than testosterone, acting with mixed antagonist and weak agonist behaviour.
quick.risks: Human safety is unstudied and it has no approved use.
